input_signals.name: Acquisitive Growth Without Earned Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: Inorganic expansion by firms that have not accumulated retained earnings—i.e., firms with no track record of internally funded profit—is the archetype of low-quality growth and predicts poor returns, whereas acquisitions by seasoned, self-financed firms are more likely value-accretive.
input_signals.reasoning: Acquisition spending plus the goodwill increment isolates externally purchased growth rather than organic capex, and low retained-earnings-to-assets is a life-cycle quality marker for firms whose equity comes from issuance rather than earned profit. The multiplicative rank form fires only in the joint corner (acquisitive and unseasoned), where overpayment and later goodwill impairment risk are concentrated; COALESCE treats unreported acquisition/goodwill items as zero activity, which is the correct economic convention.

input_signals.name: Margin-Validated Capex (Signed Quality Weighting)
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment intensity is not itself directional; it amplifies the information in the trajectory of unit economics. Aggressive capex when gross profitability on assets is trending up signals capacity earning above cost, while equally aggressive capex when it is trending down signals competitive erosion and value destruction; low-investment firms carry little of either signal.

The quadrant flaw is removed by making the investment leg a nonnegative within-industry intensity weight in [0,1] and letting only the quality leg carry sign, so the ordering is high-capex/improving-margin at the top, high-capex/deteriorating-margin at the bottom, and all low-capex firms compressed near zero regardless of margin direction. This is exactly the productive-versus-unproductive investment split the hypothesis describes, and industry ranking of capex/PPE prevents sector capital-intensity cycles from driving the weight.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), zscore( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex Without Debt-Service Capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: Aggressive capital spending is safe when operating cash flow comfortably covers the existing liability stock, but the same spending by firms with thin cash-flow coverage raises refinancing and distress risk and forces later curtailment or asset sales, predicting low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the rejected external-financing wedge with legs that are not linked by the funding identity: a within-industry investment-intensity rank (a flow relative to installed capital) and a stock-based coverage ratio of smoothed operating cash flow to total liabilities. Industry ranking of capex/PPE strips sector capital-intensity differences so the conditioning is on firm-specific balance-sheet fragility rather than on being a capital-intensive industry.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ma( oancf, 3 ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Intangible-Heavy Base Without Cash Earnings
input_signals.hypothesis: A balance sheet dominated by purchased intangibles represents past investment whose value is unverified by cash generation; when the firm's operating cash flow on assets is persistently weak, that intangible stock is a write-down waiting to happen and the market underweights the impairment risk.

The mechanism is asymmetric by construction: intangible-heavy firms that do generate cash score low, which is precisely the productive-versus-unverified investment distinction.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), at ) ), rank( neg( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.hypothesis: Excess capacity in working capital is best measured as a state, not a one-year flow: when a firm's inventory-days sits at the top of its own five-year history at the same time that its gross margin is trending down, discounting has already begun and further markdowns and write-offs are coming, which the market prices with a lag.

input_signals.name: Capacity Growth Without Cash Coverage
input_signals.hypothesis: What is punished is not the level of capital intensity but the act of adding gross capacity while operating cash flow covers only a small fraction of outstanding liabilities: such firms are enlarging fixed commitments they cannot service.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates one design choice in the archive's best family — replacing the capex/PPE intensity level with the gross-PP&E growth flow while holding the cash-coverage leg fixed — which tells us whether the effect comes from being capital-heavy or from actively expanding. input_signals.hypothesis: An aged capital base (net PP&E far below gross PP&E) at a firm still generating strong operating cash flow indicates a harvesting business whose depreciation overstates true economic decay; its earnings are understated and its low reinvestment need means high free cash flow, so it earns positive abnormal returns.

input_signals.name: Cash Burn Years From Investment Deficit
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters for an investing firm is not a coverage ratio but a horizon: the annual gap between capital spending and recurring operating cash flow, expressed relative to the cash stock, measures how many years the firm can sustain its current investment program before it must raise capital or cut. input_signals.hypothesis: Investment discipline is visible in the second moment: firms whose capital spending rate is stable across five years are executing a planned program, while lumpy investors are reacting to windfalls or crises. input_signals.name: Long Assets Funded Short
input_signals.hypothesis: Heavy investment in long-lived assets financed with debt maturing inside a year creates a maturity mismatch: the cash flows from the new capacity arrive years after the obligations fall due, so when credit tightens these firms must refinance at bad terms, sell assets, or abandon projects, and returns are low.

Both legs are bounded ranks, with the investment leg industry-ranked so the sort is not simply picking capital-intensive industries.

input_signals.hypothesis: A heavily depreciated capital base depresses reported earnings through high depreciation charges while contributing little to economic decline; the market misreads this as decay. input_signals.name: Hiring While Short-Funded
input_signals.hypothesis: Headcount growth is a commitment to a recurring cash obligation, so it is as sensitive to funding structure as capital spending: firms expanding payroll while relying on debt maturing inside a year against thin liquid assets must reverse that expansion through layoffs and restructuring charges when credit tightens, and their returns are low.

input_signals.hypothesis: The impairment mechanism is a deterioration in the revenue support behind acquired intangible capital. When intangibles per dollar of sales rises — because the firm bought more intangible assets, because revenue shrank, or both — each dollar of acquired capital is supporting less business than it did a year ago, and write-downs plus strategic resets follow.

input_signals.name: Acquisitions Funded With New Long-Term Debt
input_signals.hypothesis: The financing of an acquisition determines who bears the cost of overpayment. Firms making large acquisitions while simultaneously adding long-term debt have levered the purchase price onto the equity claim, so any shortfall in the acquired business is amplified into impairment, covenant pressure, and forced divestiture.
input_signals.reasoning: Every acquisition-related signal in this archive conditions on the *adequacy* of cash flow; none conditions on the *source of funds* for the purchase itself, which is a separable economic channel — an acquirer paying from surplus cash and one issuing debt look identical on a coverage screen in the deal year. Both legs are contemporaneous flows measuring one decision, and scaling new long-term debt by the existing liability stock makes the leg a measure of how much the firm's claim structure was expanded to buy growth rather than a size effect.

input_signals.name: Growth With Habitual Self-Funding
input_signals.hypothesis: What validates expansion is not the size of one window's cash surplus but whether the firm routinely covers its capital spending out of operations. Counting how many of the past five years had operating cash flow above capital expenditure identifies habitual self-funders, and capacity growth by such firms reflects an internally imposed hurdle rather than access to accommodating capital markets.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces a deflator swap with a different functional form of the conditioner — a persistence count rather than a scaled cumulative difference — so it is not a monotone transformation of the tested asset-scaled surplus measure: a firm with one huge surplus year and four deficit years scores low here and high there. The count is also robust to lumpy investment and to scale, and it makes the economic claim explicit, namely that financing discipline is a habit that distinguishes productive from opportunistic growth.

input_signals.name: Purchased Growth Without Earned Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has accumulated no retained earnings has never demonstrated that it can earn a return on capital; when such a firm's balance sheet also carries a heavy load of purchased intangible capital per revenue dollar, its growth has been bought with outside money by management with no track record of internal value creation, and the acquired base is the most likely place for that inexperience to be revealed.
input_signals.reasoning:
This repairs the archive's earliest diagnosed failure rather than ensembling two winners: the retained-earnings life-cycle conditioner produced the strongest cross-sectional slope in the entire search (fmb −3.33) but no tradable alpha, and the diagnosis was that its investment leg — acquisition flow with a large exact-zero mass — could not form a stable extreme portfolio. Pairing that conditioner with the continuously distributed intangible-load leg tests the diagnosis directly, and the conditioner is economically independent of the cash-coverage and liquidity channels that dominate the rest of the archive because it measures cumulative earned capital rather than current cash adequacy.
